title: Psychological and neural responses to architectural interiors
research_question: 1) Can aesthetic responses to architectural scenes be reduced to a few key psychological dimensions? 2) Are these dimensions sensitive to salient design features and Global Image Properties (GIPs)? 3) Do these psychological dimensions correlate with neural activation patterns, and to what extent are these correlations modulated by task?

participants.description: Experiment 1: 798 US-based adults (391 women, 401 men, 6 other; M=38.06 years, SD=11.96). Experiment 2: 614 American adults (305 women, 307 men, 2 other; M=35.68 years, SD=10.87). Experiment 3: 18 healthy participants (12 females, 6 males; M=23.39 years, SD=4.49) from the Canary Islands.
participants.recruitment: Amazon's Mechanical Turk for Experiments 1 and 2. Not specified for Experiment 3 (reanalysis of previous fMRI studies).

stimuli_or_exposures.description: 200 images of interior architectural spaces, counterbalanced on perceived enclosure (open/closed), ceiling height (high/low), and contour (round/square). This yielded 8 experimental conditions (25 images per condition).

measures.instrument: 16 aesthetic rating scales (Complexity, Organization, Naturalness, Beauty, Personalness, Interest, Modernity, Valence, Stimulation, Vitality, Comfort, Relaxation, Hominess, Uplift, Approachability, Explorability) on a 7-point sliding semantic differential scale.
Principal Component Analysis (PCA) scores for Coherence, Hominess, and Fascination.
Self-similarity (Pyramidal Histogram of Oriented Gradients - PHOG method) and Complexity (HOG Complexity method).

findings.mechanism: Psychometric Network Analysis (PNA) revealed three communities: Coherence, Hominess, and Fascination.
findings.quote: three communities were found. Community 1 was closely associated with three aesthetic response measures (organization, modernity, and beauty)

findings.mechanism: Principal Component Analysis (PCA) identified three components: Coherence (PC1), Hominess (PC2), and Fascination (PC3).

mechanisms: Fluency theory: ordered arrangements increase efficiency of information processing, heightening aesthetic appeal (for Coherence).
Hygge concept: feelings of coziness, warmth, and togetherness from intimate spaces (for Hominess).
Attention Restoration Theory (ART): informational richness and complexity capture involuntary attention, allowing directed attention mechanisms to replenish (for Fascination).
Integration of cognitive, emotional, and sensory information: psychological experiences in the built environment are generated by the integration of these processes.
Top-down influence on object processing: neural responses in visual cortex are likely driven by top-down valuation rather than bottom-up psychophysical properties.
implementation_implications: Architects can use the identified psychological components (coherence, fascination, hominess) to test the psychological impact of proposed design schemes before construction.
These components can be used for post-occupancy evaluations of buildings to gather behavioral feedback for future interior design and construction decisions.
Architects may weigh these components differently depending on the building type (e.g., home, hospital, library, museum).

limitations: The use of two-dimensional images limits the generalizability of findings to three-dimensional built spaces.
The study focused on visual perception of architecture, being agnostic about the contribution of nonvisual senses to architectural experiences.
Only three basic architectural design variables were considered, capturing a limited proportion of a building's visual properties.
